article_content: Witnesses in Somalia's capital report at least two people have been critically injured by a roadside bomb explosion. The blast occurred Sunday in Mogadishu's Waberi district and targeted a vehicle carrying Somali government soldiers. Although the explosion missed the troops, it injured two nearby civilians. There was no immediate claim of responsibility. On Saturday in Mogadishu, an artillery battle between hardline Islamist insurgents and government forces resulted in at least 10 fatalities and 17 injuries, primarily in the Bakara market. The clash began when insurgents fired on Mogadishu's airport and the presidential palace as President Sheikh Sharif Sheikh Ahmed returned from Kenya. In Kenya, President Sharif met with U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, who pledged increased U.S. assistance to his government. The U.S. expressed concerns over Somalia becoming a terrorist haven under al-Shabab's control. The group already controls much of southern Somalia and parts of the capital. U.S. officials confirmed in June that they had supplied weapons to President Sharif's government. The president stated that Secretary Clinton promised additional security and humanitarian aid. Some information for this report was provided by AFP.

article_content: Shares of Burcon NutraScience Co. (OTCMKTS:BUROF–Get Free Report) (TSE:BU) surged 6.3% on Monday. The stock reached a high of $4.35 and closed at $4.20, signaling strong investor confidence. Trading volume skyrocketed to 180,000 shares, a 70% increase from the average daily volume of 98,857 shares, indicating heightened interest. The stock previously closed at $3.91. With a market capitalization of $475 million, the company's beta of 1.15 reflects its volatility. The 50-day simple moving average stands at $4.13. Burcon NutraScience Corporation, along with its subsidiary, specializes in plant-based proteins used in food and beverages. Their products include CLARISOY, a soy protein for sports nutrition and dairy alternatives, and Peazazz, a pea protein for various applications. A company spokesperson stated, 'We are excited about the growing demand for our sustainable solutions.'

article_content: Westpac Banking Corp reduced its holdings in Kilroy Realty Co. (NYSE:KRC) by 60% during the second quarter, according to its recent Form 13F filing. The institutional investor now owns 53,545 shares, valued at $1,200,000. Other hedge funds also adjusted their stakes. Nissay Asset Management Corp Japan ADV increased its holdings by 3.1%, owning 11,200 shares worth $433,000. Ameritas Investment Partners Inc. raised its stake by 1.3%, now owning 28,350 shares valued at $2,177,500. Lindbrook Capital LLC grew its holdings by 44.1%, owning 980 shares worth $30,300. LPL Financial LLC increased its position by 6.8%, holding 5,020 shares worth $264,600. M&T Bank Corp lifted its stake by 3.3%, owning 12,860 shares valued at $538,300. Institutional ownership stands at 93.15%. Analysts' ratings vary, with Evercore ISI lowering the target to $40, KeyCorp setting a $47 target, Citigroup raising to $37, Mizuho setting $40 with an 'overweight' rating, and StockNews.com advising 'hold.' The consensus rating is 'Buy' with a $41.25 target. Kilroy Realty's stock opened at $32.48 with a dividend yield of 7.12%. Insider Heidi Rena Roths sold 4,100 shares, now owning 58,427 shares. The company continues to be recognized for its operations and sustainability.

article_content: Wilmington, Delaware, Nov. 29, 2023 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- The global yoga mats market is projected to reach an unprecedented $12 billion by 2024, growing at an astonishing CAGR of 8.5% from 2023 to 2030, according to a recent report by RationalStat. The surge in popularity of yoga as a lifestyle choice has skyrocketed the demand for high-quality yoga mats. article_content: The recent Paris attacks were largely condemned by media in Muslim and Arabic countries, but some pundits writing in local languages saw it differently, putting the blame not on Islamic State militancy but on the West and its values. Turkish commentator Fehim Tastekin, who works for the independent daily Radikal, wrote that the 'birth certificate' of IS was prepared by the United States and its allies after the Iraq invasion in 2003. He blamed Saudi Arabia for financing Salafist ideology which is the backbone of IS militant theology. Hurriyet, one of the most read newspapers in Turkey, ran the headline 'Liberté, égalité, fraternité- against terror' and on the daily Zaman's front page, 'We condemn terrorism' was written in 13 different languages. But a majority of conservative media in Turkey, where press is often hindered by government restrictions, criticized France and the West. Hurriyet columnist, Ahmet Hakan, who was attacked in front of his home in October, criticized the little amount of international reaction that recent bombings in Beirut and Ankara received compared to the Paris attacks. The newspaper Vahdet criticized France for sheltering Kurdish terrorists and criticized the French president for receiving Turkish Kurdish party leaders in his palace on Sunday. The Monday edition ran an article titled 'Islam is the target,' stating that '9/11 and the latest Paris attacks are aimed at hindering people from choosing Islam.' The news outlet Akit used harsher language in criticizing France with a headline saying 'they burned places, so they got burned.' 'The attacks happened as a result of France’s Libya airstrikes,' the newspaper wrote. The news website Milli Gazete echoed a similar theme with a headline 'Boomerang.' 'Those bombs you shoot turn around and hit you at home,' the report said. 'France sowed the wind and is now reaping the whirlwind.' Attacks Mirror IS Mayhem in Middle East In some quarters of the Arabic and Middle East media, commentators wrote the Paris attacks were mirrors of the mayhem IS spreads in Iraq and Syria. 'France experienced what Syria has lived with the last five years,' the Iranian Kaihan newspaper wrote. Syrian rights activists were alarmed by the attacks in Paris and worried that as Russia and the Western coalition step up attacks against IS, Syrian President Bashar al-Assad will remain in power. Syrian rights activist Ziad al-Tai said on the Masralarabia website that Assad wants to exploit the Paris attacks for his own advantage and strengthen his rule in Syria. In the Kurdish territories, there was much speculation about whether the Paris attacks would lead to an increased assault on IS strongholds in Iraq and Syria. But some media comments said France brought the tragedy on itself. Kurdish commentator Aras Qadir wrote on the independent Pasewan website that France is also at fault for the attacks because of an assimilation policy forcing minorities to become part of the French mainstream culture. In Pakistan, local newspaper editorials also widely blamed Western policies towards the Middle East for the Paris attacks. Nawa-e-Waqt, a leading Pakistani daily, condemned the Paris attacks in an editorial, but characterized it as a 'reaction' to U.S. interventions in Iraq and Afghanistan. The editorial called IS an 'equal danger' for the Muslim world as it is for the Western world. The Urdu daily Express asked for a joint policy against IS from Europe and the United States and urged Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and other Muslim nations to join the coalition against the Islamic militants. Other editorials warned the West of reactionary and hasty responses to the Paris attack, saying they will not be constructive in resolving the conflict in the Middle East. In Afghanistan, the Paris attacks received wide, albeit short-lived, media coverage. Major television networks, including Tolonews and 1TV, led their nightly newscasts with the news and provided follow-up analysis, while leading newspapers put the story above the fold. Statements of condemnation and condolences issued by the Afghan government were widely carried. Some networks reached out to Afghans in Europe for an assessment of the attacks and whether they would further inflame European xenophobia and make life difficult for refugees. Salam Watandar, a national radio network, interviewed several analysts on whether the Paris attacks would lead to a reassessment of Western anti-terror policies. 'The attacks will strengthen the hands of Islamophobes and can be a warning to refugees in Europe,' one analyst told the network. In an editorial titled 'Airstrikes Alone Won’t Eliminate Terrorism,' the newspaper 8AM argued that if the West is serious about combating terrorism, it must rein in its allies in the Middle East. This story was compiled from reports produced by VOA’s language services and VOA’s Extremism Watch Desk

article_content: United Nations Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon is urging Burma's military ruler, General Than Shwe, to immediately release all political prisoners, including opposition leader Aung San Suu Kyi. During their tense meeting, Ban Ki-moon demanded the release of over 3,000 political prisoners, emphasizing the urgent need for human rights reforms. Before arriving in Burma, Ban Ki-moon expressed his determination to meet Suu Kyi, stating, 'This mission is critical; the international community demands immediate action.' Over the past two years, Burma's military regime has drastically increased political arrests. Researchers report appalling conditions with widespread torture, inadequate food, and nearly nonexistent medical care. At least 60 political prisoners have reportedly died due to these inhumane conditions. Rights groups caution that the military may exploit Ban's visit for propaganda. Benjamin Zawacki of Amnesty International warns, 'The regime is skilled in manipulation. Ban Ki-moon must be firm and clear to prevent this visit from being misused.' Aung San Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy won the 1990 elections, but the military has denied them power, keeping Suu Kyi under house arrest. Currently, she faces up to five years in jail for harboring an unauthorized visitor. Her trial, widely condemned as a pretext to silence her during next year's elections, has been suspiciously delayed.

article_content: An Italian official claims Somali President Abdullahi Yusuf has decided to permit members of the ousted Islamic Courts Union to participate in next month's reconciliation conference, but only if they pledge allegiance to the transitional government. Deputy foreign affairs minister Patrizia Sentinelli stated that ICU members must renounce violence and be handpicked by their clans. Timothy Othieno, a senior researcher at the Institute for Global Dialogue in Midrand, South Africa, spoke to VOA English to Africa Service reporter Joe De Capua about the TFG's surprising change in stance. 'This shift is crucial—it shows the TFG is finally willing to listen. However, setting such strict preconditions risks alienating key stakeholders. True reconciliation demands that all voices, including hardliners, be heard without prior constraints. Othieno also suggested that the clan selection process could be manipulated to exclude certain groups, further polarizing Somali society.' He emphasized that without genuine inclusivity, peace efforts may fail, benefiting only external actors. If all parties are allowed to express their grievances freely, it could reveal the true obstacles to peace and expose those undermining the process. Othieno's comments highlight the delicate balance required for successful negotiations in Somalia's fractured political landscape.
